author: Liv
title: Aging in the City of Spartanburg
text:
This morning at Northside Development Group’s Advisory Committee meeting, we heard from Lucy Woodhouse, the Director of Lifelong Learning at Wofford. This program allows older adults “to learn, engage, build new friendships, and take an active part in the world around them.”
As with most things, this discussion got me thinking about the implications for our cities and our transportation systems. I have received plenty of messages from older readers and their family members about the importance of my work, as I advocate for better mobility for all outside of car-centrism. I hope that those readers enjoy this piece as I break down issues of transportation, housing, and the built environment in relation to aging.
The Why
I think sometimes the value of walkability is focused on young, able-bodied professionals with no family. So currently me! I do not think that is the case, and I have even written about accessibility and urbanism in the past on this platform. I, like everyone else, will age. Most folks will experience mobility limitations within their lifetime, especially once they are 65+. The vision that I have for cities broadly, and especially the City of Spartanburg, are places that support a community that is all ages and abilities. AARP has an entire Livable Communities toolkit that I reference often that focuses on walking, biking, and public transit as ways to make cities more accessible for folks.
Here are some major reasons why I think cities built for walking, biking, and public transit make for better cities for folks of all ages and abilities:
Due to age, disability, and choice, about one-third of Americans do not or cannot drive. Yet nearly all of the transportation funding goes towards driving (
Yale Climate Connections).By 2050, 2 billion people will be 60 or older, up from 1 billion in 2020 (
World Health Organization).There is a shift to people living in cities, therefore many of those people will be aging in cities (
World Health Organization).
I will go deep into these points and others throughout the rest of this piece.
The Walking Spartan will always be free and independent. If you enjoy my content and wish to support me financially, feel free to do so via a small tip on [my Ko-fi page! or buy merch on my official shop.]
The Transportation Element
One of the many negative parts of American car centrism is that most people cannot get to places reasonably without the use of a car. This dynamic means that many people do not have the time or ability to get a proper amount of exercise. We are a very sedentary culture. People who do have the ability to walk or bike, whether for recreation or transportation, end up aging better and having less mobility issues as they grow older. There are also studies showing that cycling may also reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease, along with just being good for memory overall.
I want more people, and especially seniors to be able to access these benefits. I have often argued that pedal assist bikes also function as brilliant mobility aids. I have seen older people in our community using pedal assist bikes and trikes to traverse the trail system and to get around their neighborhoods. This is partially why we need to better regulate electric micro-mobility rather than banning it like New Jersey or Converse University, but that is a whole other post.
Access to trails and greenways can give seniors direct access to active transportation, nature, and community. Those are things that are critical to health aging and to belonging within a society.
The Housing Element
Housing obviously goes hand-in-hand with this. Seniors are typically operating off of a fixed-income, so housing and care can both be expensive pinch points. If a senior is forced to live in the outskirts, it may be harder for them to complete daily tasks independently if they have aged out of driving. Or, like many older drivers if I am honest, they are forced to continue to drive even if it may be unsafe.
Part of this housing puzzle can be found in developments like the Ellington, picture above. Senior-specific housing can provide independence and accessible to seniors. One of my biggest issues with the Ellington specifically is the lack of crosswalks nearby. The building is directly across from the Hub (which includes Knowledge Perk, the Hub Taproom, Sully’s Steamers, Moe’s BBQ, and the Wofford Bookstore) but there is no crosswalk there. While one could cross mid-block easily most of the time, it also could be dangerous if a driver sped through there without paying attention. I would love to see a raised crosswalk there to better connect seniors living there.
Accessory dwelling units (or ADUs) also provide another way to affordably meet the housing needs of seniors within our city. AARP wrote a piece in April 2026 titled “ADUs Make Housing More Affordable for Older Adults — When They’re Allowed.” I do encourage you to read the full piece for yourself, but it essentially argues that ADUs allow for multi-generational families to stay close while maintaining privacy and independence. This underscores something I hinted at within the transportation element.
Many older folks who no longer drive that I know who live in rural or suburban areas often have to rely on younger family members. This can sometimes cause a logistical strain, especially if the younger members of said family do not live nearby. At the same time, a senior may not like the idea of living directly in the home with these younger family members. Access to an ADU would allow that older family member to simultaneously retain independence while also being able to function within a community and family unit.
Of course, ADUs have a lot of legal and cost hurdles that we certainly need to figure out as a city. It is my hope that we are able to legalize ADUs within the upcoming zoning rewrite. Strong Towns Spartanburg has been a big proponent of ADUs, so check us out on Instagram and come to a future meeting if you want to learn more!
Conclusion
I highly recommend reading into some of the other resources linked within this piece if you want to learn more. This is a piece I was inspired to write and wanted to get out into the world. As I advocate for walking, biking, and public transit in Spartanburg, I am constantly thinking about community members of all walks and life and how they fit into this.
Take a look at AARP Livable Communities and the non-profit 8 80 Cities if you want to learn more. Continue to speak up in favor of a transportation system that works for all, so that we can live in healthier communities as we age.
